items.stem: If y varies inversely as x and x is doubled, what happens to y?
items.markingKey: C. y = k/x, so y becomes k/(2x) = y/2.

items.stem: In a model, the intensity of light y varies directly as the square of x, where x is the distance from the source. Explain what happens to y when x is multiplied by 3, and justify your answer algebraically.

items.stem: Explain why the maximum of h(t) = at² + bt + c with a < 0 occurs at t = −b/(2a).

items.stem: Explain why Newton's law of cooling is modelled by T = A + Be^(−kt) rather than by a linear function.
items.answer: The rate of cooling is proportional to the temperature difference with the room, so cooling is fast at first and slows down; this gives exponential decay of the difference towards the asymptote T = A, not a constant rate.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: The rate of cooling is proportional to the temperature difference with the room, so cooling is fast at first and slows down; this gives exponential decay of the difference towards the asymptote T = A, not a constant rate. items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of this view: "A mathematical model is only useful if its predictions are exactly correct."

Arguments against: all models simplify reality ("all models are wrong, some are useful"); approximate models still guide decisions and reveal trends; models can be refined over the modelling cycle. items.stem: Give one argument for and one argument against this view: "A mathematical model is only useful if its predictions are exactly correct."
items.answer: Models are useful when their accuracy is adequate for their purpose and their limitations are understood; exactness is neither possible nor necessary.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: inaccurate models can mislead decisions; testing against data is essential. Arguments against: all models simplify reality ("all models are wrong, some are useful"); approximate models still guide decisions and reveal trends; models can be refined over the modelling cycle. Supported judgement: Models are useful when their accuracy is adequate for their purpose and their limitations are understood; exactness is neither possible nor necessary.
